Green hydrogen could supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050. Yet today, less than 1% of production is low-carbon, and much of the investment remains concentrated away from many of the Global South’s lowest-cost production regions.

The question is not only whether green hydrogen can scale, but whether it will strengthen national development and improve people’s lives, or primarily serve external energy demand.

For countries in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East, green hydrogen offers real opportunities: supporting industrial development, creating jobs, strengthening energy security, and diversifying economies. Some estimates suggest that hydrogen-related value chains could generate hundreds of thousands of jobs in emerging markets if local industries and skills are developed. But without careful planning, it risks repeating extractive models where resources are exported while local value creation remains limited.

Producing 1 kg of green hydrogen can require around 9 liters of purified water, meaning that large-scale projects may demand millions of cubic meters of water in regions that are already water-stressed. Land requirements are also significant: producing 1 million tons of hydrogen can require around 30,000 hectares of solar capacity, raising important questions about land use and ecosystem protection.

This is why UNDP , together with the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, developed the 3P framework — People, Planet, and Prosperity. The framework helps ensure that hydrogen strategies align with national development priorities, operate within ecological limits, and generate shared economic benefits.
I will be discussing these issues at the European Hydrogen Energy Conference (EHEC) (EHEC 2026) in Seville on 12 March, during Plenary Session 3: Energy Security Profiles for the Global Transition.
